items.note: Local name, in quotes, listed apart from Common Gull and Black-backed Gull. 'Grey Gull' was commonly used for immature large gulls (Herring or Great Black-backed) or for Herring Gull. Kittiwake (Rissa) can't be ruled out.

The quotes suggest a keeper's local name, not necessarily Little Gull (Hydrocoloeus minutus), which would be unlikely as a resident. It could be Black-headed Gull or Kittiwake. If the committee's text uses it without quotes elsewhere, consider Hydrocoloeus minutus.

'Royal Gull' points to the larger bird, probably Great Black-backed Gull (Larus marinus), but 'Black-backed' alone could also be Lesser Black-backed Gull (L. fuscus). Raise to L. marinus if the station's context supports it.
Victorian 'Hawks' covers falcons as well as accipiters. Dark grey suggests adult male Merlin, Sparrowhawk or Hen Harrier. It doesn't fit one family.
Assumes a true diver (loon). Keepers sometimes used 'Diver' loosely for any diving seabird (grebes, auks), so check the context; the example has none.
OCR garble of 'Fringillidae'. In the Victorian sense this family also took in buntings and sparrows (now Emberizidae and Passeridae), so the modern family is narrower than what was meant.
The text glosses it as Common Gull. 'Megs' is probably 'Mews' (cf. Mew Gull = L. canus). Keepers' 'Common Gull' sometimes meant Herring Gull or Kittiwake, so check the station.
'Large White ... Gulls that hatched here', kept apart from 'Grey-backed Gulls' (probably Herring Gull). It could be Great Black-backed Gull or Herring Gull. Unclear.
'the larger ones at odd times for the big drum' doesn't name a bird. Check the full sentence. It may not refer to birds at all (the fog-signal drum?).
Unreadable OCR heading ('SItviInz.'). 'August 19th and 27th, singles' fits Swifts, Shrikes or similar. Check the page image.
Paired with A. pratensis, so this is Anthus trivialis. Note the committee's claim of a 'great rush' of Tree Pipits.
Unidentified uncommon gulls. The full passage may say which kind.
'one white bird' in a passing flock of Sparrows. Probably a leucistic or albino sparrow, possibly a Snow Bunting. Can't tell.

notes: Check: (1) 2450-2452 and 2459: the quoted local gull names. 'Grey' Gull, 'Little' Gull, 'Royal Gull' and 'Large White' versus 'Grey-backed' should be read against the station's other entries before narrowing them below genus or family. (2) 2458: confirm 'Megs' = Mews and the Common Gull gloss. (3) 2462 'SItviInz.' and 2460 'larger ones': look at the page images. (4) 2464: Tree Pipit in a 'great rush' with Meadow Pipit may reflect the committee's identification and be worth flagging. (5) 2455 Diver: check whether the keeper used it loosely for any diving seabird. (6) 2456: Victorian Fringillidae was wider than the modern family.
